tldr: A single policy enables a humanoid to get up autonomously after falling and resume its locomotion task without any mode switching. The keys are routing behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors (AMP) based on robot posture and refining reference motions in simulation beforehand.
hero_caption: The overall ReLoco framework. Human motion capture data is refined in simulation to generate expert trajectories. By switching motion priors (AMP) and task rewards based on robot posture, a single proprioceptive policy learns locomotion and fall recovery simultaneously.
overview:
Autonomous fall recovery is an essential capability for humanoid robots operating in the real world. However, upright smooth walking/running and getting up from the ground using the arms and full body involve entirely different contact states and body mechanics. Conventional reinforcement learning has either used separate controllers for locomotion and get-up switched by state machines, or mixed both behaviors into a single adversarial motion prior (AMP: a framework combining imitation learning and reinforcement learning to encourage natural motions resembling expert data). However, the former frequently fails at switching boundaries, while the latter severely degrades locomotion tracking accuracy.

To resolve this dilemma, the authors propose "ReLoco", a unified framework equipped with "behavior-conditioned AMP" that dynamically switches reference data and discriminator output heads based on robot posture (torso height and tilt). During training, the system automatically determines whether the robot is fallen or upright. It samples from either recovery or locomotion expert libraries while evaluating motion naturalness using a shared feature representation and behavior-specific heads in the discriminator. Furthermore, instead of using human motion capture data as-is, they convert it offline into "simulation-refined motions" that comply with robot joint limits and contact models to serve as expert data.

Evaluation results show that the policy achieves a 96.96% push-recovery success rate (including command resumption) in simulation, matching dedicated recovery controllers in get-up performance while maintaining high-precision velocity tracking. In addition, the policy was deployed directly to the 64.5-kg "Tiangong 3.0" humanoid robot. A single neural network demonstrated walking and running on paved roads, grass, and slopes, autonomous get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and smooth running resumption after being kicked down while running.
contributions: Achieved both locomotion tracking and fall recovery with command resumption within a single policy, using behavior-conditioned AMP that selects reference pools based on robot posture and scores motions with a shared feature extractor and separate heads.
Established a simulation-based refinement method that converts retargeted human motion data into robot-executable reference motions satisfying contact and torque limits beforehand.

Demonstrated locomotion across diverse terrains, get-up from arbitrary postures, and running resumption after disturbance-induced falls on the 64.5-kg full-sized humanoid "Tiangong 3.0" using a single policy, without controller switching or on-robot fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Why solve locomotion and fall recovery with a single policy?
sections.summary: Humanoids walking in the real world must get up and resume commanded locomotion after being knocked down by disturbances. The core challenge of this work is integrating upright walking and ground recovery—behaviors with drastically different contacts and postures—into one policy without mode switching.
sections.details:
When humanoid robots navigate workspaces or outdoor terrains, falling due to tripping over obstacles or severe disturbances is inevitable. To sustain autonomous activity, the robot must use its limbs to support itself from the ground, stand up, and resume tracking the velocity command given before the fall.

However, these two behaviors have opposite dynamical properties. Locomotion requires maintaining an upright posture while switching foot contacts regularly. In contrast, fall recovery is a rugged full-body motion involving curling up, pushing against the ground with the arms, and twisting the torso significantly. Traditionally, separate policies were trained for each behavior and switched via state-transition logic, but this often led to switching failures in transitional, half-fallen states or during the unstable moments right after standing up.

Adversarial motion priors (AMP), which learn natural behaviors from human demonstrations, do not enforce strict frame-by-frame trajectory tracking. This makes it easier to generate recovery motions even from unexpected postures caused by disturbances. However, naively mixing locomotion and recovery data into a single AMP broadens the demonstration distribution too much, sacrificing delicate velocity tracking performance during locomotion.

To tackle this challenge, this paper proposes the "ReLoco" framework. By separating training reference data and discriminator output heads according to robot posture (upright vs. fallen), and pre-refining human motion data into robot-executable trajectories inside a physics simulator, the framework seamlessly accommodates both high-precision locomotion and robust fall recovery within a single proprioceptive policy.

sections.heading: Posture-based routing and reference motion refinement
sections.summary: The system determines behavior state from torso height and tilt, dynamically switching the AMP reference pool and task rewards. Additionally, an offline refinement pipeline fixes discrepancies in human motion within simulation.
sections.details:
ReLoco's learning system consists of two stages: simulation-based motion refinement (Stage 1) and unified policy training with behavior-conditioned AMP (Stage 2).

### II-A Problem Formulation and Policy Setup
The overall system is formulated as a Markov Decision Process and trained using Asymmetric Actor-Critic (where the actor uses only observable information for inference, while the critic uses privileged information during value learning). Actor inputs consist solely of proprioceptive information: joint angles, joint angular velocities, torso gyroscope and gravity projection vectors, previous actions, and velocity commands. Policy outputs are offsets to default joint positions, converted to target joint torques via a PD controller. A binary routing label indicating whether the robot is upright ($b_t=0$) or fallen/recovering ($b_t=1$) is used only during training and is not provided during real-robot deployment.

### II-B Behavior-Conditioned Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP) Design
To govern supervision during training, the label $b_t$ is determined from torso height $h_t$ (threshold 0.9 m) and vertical posture alignment $u_t$ (threshold 0.7).
- **Discriminator Architecture**: Taking the past 10 frames (each with 76-dimensional motion features plus a 1-dimensional condition label $\mathbf{c}_t=[b_t]$) as input, a shared feature extraction network $F_{\phi_F}$ is followed by two scalar output heads: an upright head $H_{\phi_0}$ and a recovery head $H_{\phi_1}$. This allows learning a shared motion representation while scoring behavior-specific styles separately.
- **Task Reward Separation and Regularization**: An upright state receives velocity-tracking rewards, whereas fall recovery receives a torso-height lifting reward. Meanwhile, penalties on joint torques, accelerations, action rates, and joint limits are applied constantly in both modes as shared regularization terms.
- **Policy Optimization**: PPO is used. Since reward scales differ between upright and recovery states, the authors introduce route-specific advantage normalization to normalize advantages independently for each behavior route, stabilizing training.

### II-C Simulation-Based Reference Motion Refinement
Data obtained from kinematic retargeting of human motion capture often contains foot slipping, joint limit violations, and unnatural self-collisions. Therefore, prior to training, a tracking policy is used to execute the human motions on the robot inside the simulator. Only trajectories executed under torque and contact constraints are collected to form a "refined library", which serves as expert data for AMP.

### II-D & II-E Training Strategy and Real-Robot Transfer
To encourage recovery exploration, Reference State Initialization (RSI) initializes episodes across various fallen postures upon reset. In early training, an upward assisting force (up to 400 N) pulls the head, decaying gradually to zero once the recovery success rate exceeds 80%. Random translational and rotational velocity pulse disturbances are applied during locomotion to induce falls. For sim-to-real transfer, extensive domain randomization covers actuator response delays and inertial parameters.

captions.F1: Overview of ReLoco training and deployment. In Stage 1 on the left, human motion capture data is refined inside physical simulation. In Stage 2 in the center, a single policy is trained with posture-conditioned AMP and task rewards. On the right, during real-robot deployment, neither the discriminator nor an external mode switcher is needed; all behaviors are executed autonomously using only velocity commands and proprioception.

sections.heading: Simulation validation and durability/recovery tests on the physical Tiangong 3.0
sections.summary: Ablations show that conditional AMP and reference motion refinement substantially improve velocity tracking and get-up success rates. Physical experiments demonstrate locomotion/running across diverse outdoor terrains and fully autonomous recovery from violent kicks from all directions.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted on the full-sized humanoid "Tiangong 3.0" (height 1.70 m, weight 64.5 kg, 23 actuated degrees of freedom).

### III-B Effects of Reference Motion Refinement
Comparing 43 motion sequences showed that simulation refinement reduced foot slipping and joint limit violation rates to below 1%, while decreasing body jerk by 35.5%. When using this refined data for AMP training, the mean task reward improved from 22.0 to 25.5 compared to unrefined data, and logged get-up success rates significantly improved from ~85% to ~95%.

### III-C Simulation Ablations and Performance Comparisons
Ablation experiments at 20,000 iterations (Table V) highlighted the importance of each design element:
- **Task-only RL**: Yielded the lowest velocity-tracking error, but achieved a 0% independent get-up success rate.
- **Unconditional AMP**: Achieved a 92.96% get-up success rate, but motion mixing degraded torso planar velocity RMSE to 0.1982 m/s.
- **Single-Output Conditional AMP**: Improved velocity RMSE to 0.1484 m/s, but get-up success rate remained at 87.44%.
- **Ours (Two-Output Conditional AMP)**: Further reduced velocity RMSE by 14.7% to 0.1266 m/s, achieving a 96.80% get-up success rate and a 96.96% push-recovery success rate (including command resumption). Training iterations required to reach over 90% unassisted recovery success dropped by 43.4% compared to the single-output version.

Compared to a dedicated get-up controller (HoST), although HoST had a shorter recovery time (1.57 s vs. 2.02 s), the proposed unified policy achieved much smoother get-up with significantly lower mechanical work (3.1 kJ vs. 10.7 kJ) and lower peak torques.

### III-D Real-Robot Experiments
The single policy trained in simulation was directly deployed on the physical robot:
- **Outdoor Locomotion and Running**: Across cobblestone, brick paving, grass, uphill/downhill grass slopes, and a treadmill (up to 9.3 km/h), the robot performed forward, backward, lateral walking, turning, and natural transitions to running above ~1.6 m/s without explicit gait mode switching. It navigated random commands for ~10 minutes without falling.
- **Kicking Tests from Rest**: When kicked from the front, back, and sides while standing (47 trials total), excluding 8 hardware protection triggers and 5 non-fall disturbances, the robot autonomously recovered in all 34 maintained-control falls (prone, supine, lateral). Average recovery time was 2.64 seconds.
- **Falls During Locomotion and Task Resumption**: In tests where the robot was kicked while walking or running (20 trials total), it withstood the disturbance without falling in 16 trials, and got up from complete falls to resume the commanded locomotion task in 4 trials, continuing or resuming locomotion across all trials without losing control.

The robot smoothly traverses (a) cobblestone, (b) brick paving, (c) grass, (d) downhill grass slope, (e) uphill grass slope, and (f) a treadmill (up to 9.3 km/h) using the same policy without explicit gait mode switching.

sections.heading: The trade-off between tracking accuracy and recovery in unified control
sections.summary: Experimental results confirm that conditioning AMP, separating output heads, and supplying clean reference trajectories are vital for reconciling locomotion tracking precision and get-up success in one policy.
sections.details:
Task recovery means more than merely standing up and coming to rest; it includes accurately resuming the velocity command assigned before the fall. For this reason, the push-recovery test in this study rigorously evaluates velocity RMSE after standing up.

When evaluating a unified controller, velocity tracking precision and recovery robustness easily fall into a trade-off. Task-only RL provides tracking precision but fails to explore get-up, whereas unconditional AMP enables getting up but coarsens locomotion. The proposed posture routing and two-head architecture effectively resolve this trade-off, bringing out the strengths of both within a single network.

sections.heading: Summary and outlook
sections.summary: ReLoco unifies humanoid locomotion, fall recovery, and task resumption into a single proprioceptive policy through behavior-conditioned AMP and reference motion refinement. Its practicality was validated on the physical Tiangong 3.0 without additional fine-tuning.
sections.details:
This work proposed "ReLoco", which leverages behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors to achieve humanoid walking, running, fall recovery from arbitrary postures, and command resumption within a single policy.

By selecting reference pools based on robot posture, separating discriminator outputs, and introducing expert trajectories refined in simulation to meet physical constraints, the authors achieved successful sim-to-real transfer on the 64.5-kg full-sized humanoid "Tiangong 3.0". Without relying on controller switchers or on-robot fine-tuning, the framework demonstrates a resilient motor foundation that seamlessly connects routine walking/running to recovery after violent falls.

takeaways: Even for motions with drastically different contact characteristics like locomotion and recovery, using "conditional AMP" with posture-separated discriminator heads during training enables high-precision coexistence within a single policy without interference.

Because kinematically retargeted human motion capture has many discrepancies, using "refined trajectories" executed by the robot itself in simulation as expert data strongly dictates AMP training success.
In learning recovery behaviors, a curriculum that gradually decays an initial head-pulling assist force based on success rate is extremely effective in preventing premature exploration failure.
limitations: In real-robot kick and push disturbance experiments, the magnitude of the applied external force was not measured, leaving the quantitative upper bound of disturbances the robot can withstand unclarified.

Because control relies solely on proprioception without exteroceptive sensors like head cameras (vision), behaviors do not include perceiving, avoiding, or utilizing geometric environmental features such as surrounding obstacles or ledges.

Recovery behaviors could not be evaluated in severe impact trials where hardware protections were triggered (8 out of 47 trials), leaving challenges regarding mechanical and control resilience against extreme high-impact falls.
